The invention of the movable type printing press by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, Germany, around 1440, stands as one of the most transformative technological milestones in human history. While earlier forms of movable type existed in China and Korea, Gutenberg’s innovation was distinct in its mechanical efficiency and adaptability to the complex alphabet of Western European languages. By combining a screw press, lead-tin-antimony alloy for type, and oil-based ink, Gutenberg created a system that allowed for the rapid, consistent, and relatively affordable production of books.

Before the press, books were luxury items, hand-copied by scribes in monasteries. This process was slow, error-prone, and expensive, limiting literacy and access to knowledge primarily to the clergy and the wealthy elite. The introduction of the printing press shattered this monopoly on information. Within fifty years of Gutenberg’s first major work, the 42-line Bible, an estimated 20 million volumes had been printed in Europe. This exponential increase in the availability of texts fundamentally altered the social, political, and intellectual landscape of the continent.
